nodes.statement: Freud's account of the unconscious is a functional description lacking a mechanism; Lacan's project supplies the missing formal structure, so the Lacanian system is assessed by internal coherence and derivability rather than by experimental confirmation.

nodes.name: Dream incorporation
nodes.statement: External stimuli occurring during sleep — an alarm, a ringing phone — are routinely woven into the ongoing dream, in real time, mid-plot.

nodes.name: Slip disavowal
nodes.statement: A slip of the tongue is meaningful, not noise: it fits the speaker's situation, yet the speaker disowns it ('that's not what I meant to say') — so its utterance implies a speaker who is not the 'I'.

nodes.name: Mirror stage
nodes.statement: In the mirror stage, an infant whose lived body is un-gathered — parts that move without a unified command — identifies jubilantly with a mirror image that presents one whole, coordinated body all at once; the identification means 'I will be that,' not 'that is what I am.'

nodes.name: Functional versus visual unity
nodes.statement: A body is functionally unified to the degree it answers to a single command; an image is visually unified when it merely appears as one connected whole. The mirror image has visual unity, while the pre-mirror infant's lived body lacks functional unity.

nodes.name: Identificatory transfer
nodes.statement: The founding identification takes the image's visible coherence of form as proof of the body's functional coherence of control — transferring a property of the picture onto the lived body.

nodes.name: Méconnaissance
nodes.statement: The ego is constituted by méconnaissance (misrecognition): the 'I' is an identification with an image of itself that is more together than it is, a claim strictly false at its founding that can never become true, because the image always anticipates and stays ahead of the lived reality.

nodes.name: Ego as identification
nodes.statement: The ego is not a substance or a little person inside but an imaginary formation — the ongoing act of taking an external image, a form seen from outside, as oneself.

nodes.name: Ego is not the subject
nodes.statement: The ego is not the subject: the ego is an imaginary formation, whereas the subject is never an image, cannot appear in any mirror, and is not a picture of anything.

nodes.name: Return of the fragmented body
nodes.statement: Because the ego's foundation is a mismatch, the fragmented body returns whenever the image fails — in dreams of dismemberment and falling apart, and in the panic of 'falling to pieces' under stress.

nodes.name: Structural aggression
nodes.statement: Because the ego is an image occupying a place, a person who resembles me can occupy that place, so similarity triggers rivalry and aggression; the ego's aggression is structural, built into its foundation, not an accident of temperament.

nodes.name: The Imaginary
nodes.statement: The Imaginary is the register comprising images, identification, likeness, rivalry, and the ego.

nodes.name: Mirror stage as paradigm
nodes.statement: The mirror stage is a paradigm of a structure — identification with an external form — not a literal empirical claim that infants need physical mirrors; the infant's first mirrors are the mother's responding face and the whole forms the world offers up.

nodes.name: Selective identification
nodes.statement: Among photos that are equally evidential about how one looks, the flattering one is kept as 'really me' and the honest one rejected, so the identification is selective: one identifies with the better image, not with one's image as such.

nodes.name: Inside/outside gap
nodes.statement: The felt inside is structurally, not merely occasionally, messier than the presented outside; were the 'I' simply reading itself off, the two would match, and they never do.

nodes.name: Likeness-irritation
nodes.statement: A person very like oneself — same role, style, jokes — provokes a territorial irritation that wholly different people never trigger, which is intelligible only if the 'I' is a picture occupying a place that a better instance of that picture could take.

nodes.name: The disavowing 'I'
nodes.statement: The 'I' from which slips are disowned and through which the other scene leaks is the imaginary ego — a picture the person took for themselves from outside — not a given, self-transparent core.

nodes.name: Arbitrary sign
nodes.statement: The bond between a signifier and what it names is arbitrary, and no individual can change what a word means because the community holds the bond fixed — which is how an arbitrary sign is nonetheless stable.

nodes.name: Meaning without a referent
nodes.statement: Words such as 'unicorn' and 'nevertheless' are fully meaningful although no thing exists for them to be associated with, so meaning cannot require a referent.

nodes.name: Language cuts the world
nodes.statement: The world does not arrive pre-cut into categories; each language places its own cuts, so that French 'mouton' covers both sheep and mutton and Welsh 'glas' spans a region that English divides into green and blue.

nodes.name: Meaning is not association with things
nodes.statement: What fixes a word's meaning is not a bond of association to a thing in the world.

nodes.name: Differences without positive terms
nodes.statement: In language there are only differences without positive terms: a sign's meaning is what it is not, its borders drawn by neighbouring words, and its identity is a position in a system of oppositions — as a chess piece is nothing but its value in the game, unaffected by being recast in marble.

nodes.name: The sign
nodes.statement: The linguistic sign is two-sided — a signifier (the perceivable sound-image) and a signified (the concept) — with the referent, the actual thing, outside the sign entirely, bracketed by Saussure.

nodes.name: Meaning versus reference
nodes.statement: Separating meaning from reference makes the structural method possible: meaning can be studied as a closed game, as chess can be studied without regard to what the pieces are made of.

nodes.name: Self-grounding system
nodes.statement: The system of meanings is self-grounding and circular: every word is defined by other words with no non-linguistic base case, so meaning is internal to the system, position against position, all the way down, like a geometry that touches no ground outside itself.

nodes.name: Pointing cannot fix meaning
nodes.statement: Pointing at a thing cannot fix a word's meaning, because the gesture cannot specify which cut is meant — the dog, the animal, the mammal, the pet, the breed — and most of language has nothing to point at.

nodes.name: The system precedes the speaker
nodes.statement: No speaker assembles the linguistic system bottom-up; every speaker acquires an already-finished system that was in place before they existed, so what acquisition delivers is a position in the network, not a stash of associations.

nodes.name: The 'I' is spoken by language
nodes.statement: Whatever 'you' are, meaning-wise, you are made of inherited linguistic material; the 'I' that believes it speaks language is first something spoken by it, and one cannot mean anything, even in rebellion, except out of material that was already there.
aliases: the I that believes it speaks language is, first, something spoken by it

nodes.name: Selection and combination
nodes.statement: Every act of speaking simultaneously selects a word from the set of words that could occupy the slot and combines the chosen word with its neighbours into a sequence; selection and combination are the two axes on which every sentence rides.

nodes.name: Metaphor and metonymy
nodes.statement: The selection pole does its creative work as metaphor — naming a thing by something similar to it — and the combination pole as metonymy — naming a thing by something adjacent to it.
aliases: Condensation is metaphor: several thoughts are fused into a single image, one figure substituted for a whole network of thoughts because it resembles all of them at once.

Displacement is metonymy: the charge of an unbearable thought slides along the chain of associations onto a trivial neighboring element, so that contiguity itself stands in for the thing, as 'the Crown' stands in for the monarchy.

nodes.name: Aphasic dissociation of the poles
nodes.statement: Some aphasias destroy the selection pole, leaving patients able only to chain words by contiguity, while others destroy the combination pole, leaving only substitution without any sentence — showing that selection and combination are two separate machineries.

nodes.name: Two fundamental dream-work operations
nodes.statement: Freud holds condensation and displacement to be the two fundamental operations of the dream-work — the machinery itself; the remaining distortions (staging, secondary revision) presuppose them, and secondary revision is the waking mind's after-the-fact edit rather than unconscious machinery.

nodes.name: The unconscious runs on the signifier
nodes.statement: The unconscious selects by the material signifier — sounds, letters, words as things — and is indifferent to the signified (the meaning it bears); it operates on the letter, as when a patient is tormented by cabbages over her rival Frau Kohl (Kohl = cabbage) or Dora's dream turns on 'jewel box.'

nodes.name: Dream as rebus
nodes.statement: The dream is a rebus — a picture-puzzle whose elements stand for words — and is therefore something to be read, not seen through.

nodes.name: Lacan's algorithm of the sign
nodes.statement: Lacan rewrites the Saussurean sign as capital S over small s separated by a bar: the capitalized signifier leads (the machinery runs top-down from the material sound), the bar is a resistance rather than a bond, and the signified is not a partner but an effect produced late as the chain runs and never finally fixed.

nodes.name: Cogito
nodes.statement: Descartes' cogito: radical doubt cannot doubt the occurrence of thinking itself, since doubting is an instance of thinking; cogitatio ('thinking') covers the whole stream of experience — sensing, seeming, feeling, willing, doubting — so that in the act of thinking the 'I' is present to itself, and this self-transparency is the indubitable foundation on which knowledge is rebuilt.

nodes.name: I think where I am not
nodes.statement: Lacan's inversion of the cogito: 'I think where I am not; therefore I am where I do not think' — the thinking that is most one's own (the dream-work, the slip, the other scene) runs where one is not present, while the place where one is present to oneself (the ego) is precisely where no such thinking occurs.

nodes.name: The split subject
nodes.statement: The subject is not the transparent res cogitans but a split: divided between the 'I' that speaks and the circuit that speaks in it; the subject is neither the ego-image nor the unconscious machinery but the barred, proxy-structure between them, and it is split, not eliminated.

nodes.name: Signifier represents the subject for another signifier
nodes.statement: A signifier represents the subject for another signifier: the subject appears only by proxy, as a position in the signifying chain, never in person — as a knight is nothing but its position in the game; the word 'I' is the sharpest case, the language's word that never coincides with the one who speaks it.

nodes.name: The one bar
nodes.statement: The bar is a single operator marking the same structural fact in two places — in S/s it marks that the material form is cut off from any natural presence of its meaning, and in $ it marks that the subject is cut off from any present self that could coincide with its representation; both bars say that no transparency crosses the line.

nodes.name: The Symbolic
nodes.statement: The Symbolic is the register comprising everything that exists only as a position within a system — language, law, kinship, money, roles — which produces real effects (a banknote buys bread, a signed paper marries you) while existing nowhere in particular, since it is relative to positions and precedes and outlasts every individual.

nodes.name: The big Other
nodes.statement: The big Other (A, Autre) is the Symbolic order personified as a place — the place from which one is spoken and the addressee-of-last-resort, the structure itself standing in the position of guarantor rather than any person, God, or government; even a private conversation or a mathematical proof is structurally a message addressed to the Other.

nodes.name: Discourse of the Other
nodes.statement: The unconscious is the discourse of the Other: because the circuit that speaks where one is not speaks in signifiers, the very material of one's unconscious is the Other's borrowed material.

nodes.name: The little other
nodes.statement: The little other (a) is the person in front of you — rival, beloved, the mirror — the two-person register of the Imaginary; the big Other is the third that was always already there, the frame the dyad stands in.

nodes.name: Value equality as the connective mechanism
nodes.statement: Because the model has no pointers, when two rows must connect, equality of values is the only connective mechanism the model has.

nodes.name: Repeating-group representation
nodes.statement: When one thing has many of something, the model represents it as one fact per cell across separate rows with the shared identifier repeated as a value on each row — the shape that recurs as the foreign-key and junction-table patterns.

nodes.name: Heading and domain
nodes.statement: A relation's heading is its attribute names each paired with a domain — the set of values that attribute may draw from — and every attribute draws from exactly one domain.

nodes.name: Full attribute set always identifies
nodes.statement: The full attribute set of a relation always identifies a tuple, because two tuples that agreed on every attribute would be the same tuple.

nodes.name: Equality within a domain
nodes.statement: Equality comparison is well-defined only between values of the same domain; comparing an amount against a customer name is a category error, not a false statement.

nodes.name: Attribute domains enable value comparison
nodes.statement: Typing every attribute to exactly one domain is what makes value-comparison well-defined, and value-comparison is what every connection in the model — keys and joins alike — is built from.

nodes.name: Superkey
nodes.statement: A superkey is an attribute set that identifies every tuple in every possible state — no two tuples ever agree on all of its attributes; 'in every possible state' makes it a claim, not a survey of the rows currently present.

nodes.name: Key existence is a theorem
nodes.statement: Every relation has at least one candidate key: its full attribute set is a superkey, and removing attributes until identification dies must stop at a candidate key — so key existence follows from set-hood rather than being a rule the model imposes.

nodes.name: Primary key as designation
nodes.statement: Primary key is a designation, not a different kind of thing: choosing one of several candidate keys as primary is convention, and its real content is announcing which attributes the schema treats as the relation's identifier and having the database enforce that claim by rejecting any insert that would repeat the attribute combination.

nodes.name: SQL PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE
nodes.statement: The model has one notion, the candidate key; SQL splits the job into PRIMARY KEY (the designated key, meaning UNIQUE + NOT NULL) and UNIQUE (how every other candidate key is enforced), so all key claims are enforced even though only one gets the title.

nodes.name: UNIQUE and NULL
nodes.statement: In standard SQL, UNIQUE permits repeated NULLs (NULL is not equal to anything, itself included), so a nullable column cannot serve as a real key in practice — a SQL wrinkle, not a model one.

nodes.name: Key as strongest functional dependency
nodes.statement: A key is the strongest special case of a functional dependency: X is a superkey exactly when X → every attribute of R, a candidate key is the same with nothing removable from X, and a general FD is X → Y for some attribute set Y.

nodes.name: Direction of a functional dependency
nodes.statement: A functional dependency is an arrow, not an equation: X → Y says nothing about Y → X, so each direction must be established as its own fact about the domain.

nodes.name: SQL cannot enforce general FDs
nodes.statement: SQL cannot enforce a general functional dependency: its constraint vocabulary covers keys, foreign references, and row-local CHECKs, but 'same X, same Y' spans multiple rows, which no mainstream engine lets a check reach.

nodes.name: Hidden system identifier
nodes.statement: A hidden system-generated row identifier is a physical row address invisible to the data model; because its meaning lives outside the value layer, using it to distinguish rows rebuilds the forbidden pointer and violates the Information Principle.

nodes.name: Identity as a visible value column
nodes.statement: When two rows must be distinguished, the model's answer is a value column (a purchase_id, a receipt number, or a sufficiently fine timestamp), not a hidden identifier, so that the rows differ by value and set-hood is preserved.

nodes.name: Relation, tuple, attribute vs. table, row, column
nodes.statement: In the relational model a relation is a table, a tuple is a row, and an attribute is a column; SQL kept the table/row/column vocabulary while the theory kept relation/tuple/attribute.

nodes.name: Vector space (over ℝ)
nodes.statement: A vector space over ℝ is a set V equipped with an addition u+v∈V and a scaling cv∈V (c∈ℝ) satisfying eight laws: (1) u+v=v+u, (2) (u+v)+w=u+(v+w), (3) a zero element with v+0=v, (4) every v has a negative with v+(−v)=0, (5) 1v=v, (6) (cd)v=c(dv), (7) c(u+v)=cu+cv, (8) (c+d)v=cv+dv.
aliases: a set with two operations — addition of elements and scaling by numbers — satisfying the eight vector-space laws

nodes.name: Abelian group plus compatible scaling
nodes.statement: The eight vector-space laws compress into exactly two ideas: laws 1–4 say (V,+) is an abelian group (commutative, associative, with a zero and negatives), and laws 5–8 say the scaling respects that group structure by composing and distributing; 'linearity of the operations' means precisely laws 5–8.
aliases: (V,+) is an abelian group and scaling respects that group structure

nodes.name: Linear-combination fuel
nodes.statement: A vector space's two operations and eight laws are exactly what a linear combination v=c1v1+⋯+ckvk consumes; forming combinations uses nothing beyond addition and scaling.
aliases: linear combinations burn nothing but addition and scaling

nodes.name: Transfer of combination-based results
nodes.statement: Every concept built from linear combinations (span, independence, basis) and every theorem proved about them transfers intact to any set that supplies two operations satisfying the eight laws — ℝⁿ, matrices, polynomials, functions — so demanding more structure would only shrink the roster of examples without proving anything extra.

nodes.name: Element multiplication is undefined
nodes.statement: In a vector space, multiplication of two elements is not optional but undefined — the expression xy has no meaning — so the question 'does every nonzero element have a multiplicative inverse?' is not answered no but is unaskable until extra structure (a field or algebra) is installed on top.
aliases: a vector space's elements form a group under addition, where inverse means negative; multiplicative inverses are a field concept with no counterpart here

nodes.name: Laws decide membership
nodes.statement: Vector-space membership is decided by the eight laws alone, not by the familiarity of an operation's name: operations with unfamiliar names — e.g. 'addition' x⊕y=xy and 'scaling' c⊙x=xᶜ on the positive reals — form a vector space exactly when they satisfy the laws, so the decision procedure is a cheapest-first checklist (closure under both operations, then zero, then negatives, then the scaling laws) rather than intuition.
aliases: the eight laws do not care what the operations look like
selecting by the familiarity of an operation's name instead of by the eight laws is the failure mode

nodes.name: Arithmetic laws are identities
nodes.statement: The six arithmetic vector-space laws are identities — each asserts the equality of two expressions built from elements — so when those expressions are computed with the same operations they hold automatically in any subset of V, and an identity cannot know that a subset exists; only the possibility of an operation leaving the subset is genuinely new.
aliases: an identity cannot know that W exists

nodes.name: Subspace test
nodes.statement: A subset W of a vector space V is itself a vector space under the same operations exactly when it is nonempty, closed under addition, and closed under scaling; checking 0∈W first is a useful one-line canary that disqualifies failures instantly but is not an independent requirement.
aliases: nonempty, closed under addition, closed under scaling

nodes.name: Closure manufactures zero and negatives
nodes.statement: Within a subspace, closure under scaling alone produces the zero and the negatives: 0=0w∈W and −w=(−1)w∈W for any w∈W, so zero and negatives need not be checked separately.

nodes.name: Linear condition
nodes.statement: A linear condition is a statement L(v)=0 where L is additive (L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)) and homogeneous (L(cv)=cL(v)) — i.e. a weighted sum of the coordinates and nothing more.
aliases: L(v)=0 with L additive and homogeneous

nodes.name: Solutions of a homogeneous linear condition form a subspace
nodes.statement: The solution set of a homogeneous linear condition L(v)=0 is a subspace, because L is linear: L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)=0+0=0 and L(cv)=cL(v)=0; but the same condition set equal to a nonzero constant, L(v)=1, is an affine slice — a translate of a subspace — never a subspace, since L(u+v)=1+1=2 escapes immediately.
aliases: homogeneous linear condition → subspace; nonzero constant → affine slice
a linear condition set equal to a nonzero constant is a translate of a subspace

nodes.name: Nonlinear conditions fail closure
nodes.statement: A condition that is nonlinear in the entries is not a subspace: {det A=0} fails closure because diag(1,0)+diag(0,1)=I with det I=1≠0 — two singular matrices summing to an invertible one — consistent with det being degree 2 in the entries, so no linearity is available to save closure.
aliases: two singular matrices summing to an invertible one

nodes.name: Canonical vector spaces inherit laws from ℝ
nodes.statement: ℝⁿ (componentwise operations), ℝ^{m×n} matrices (entrywise: (A+B)_{ij}=a_{ij}+b_{ij}, (cA)_{ij}=c·a_{ij}), polynomials (coefficientwise), and functions ℝ→ℝ (pointwise: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x), (cf)(x)=c·f(x)) are all vector spaces; each of the eight laws is verified entry by entry and reduces to a law of real numbers, so these coordinatewise structures inherit their laws from ℝ, and each is an abelian group under its addition because (ℝ,+) is.
aliases: coordinatewise structures inherit their laws from ℝ
one proof for all four rows at once

nodes.name: Matrix multiplication is extra structure
nodes.statement: Matrix multiplication is not the addition of the matrix vector space but extra structure nowhere mentioned in the eight laws; judged as an addition it fails immediately, since AB≠BA in general, its identity is I rather than the zero matrix, AB can be the zero matrix with both factors nonzero, and most matrices have no multiplicative inverse.
aliases: matrix multiplication is present only when explicitly written; the vector-space operations are entrywise

nodes.name: Matrix as point and as action
nodes.statement: A matrix has two faces that are the same object: a point in a vector space (an m×n matrix is mn independent coordinates, its entries, freely added and scaled entrywise) and an action (rows times columns, transforming vectors) — and the subject's power comes from switching between them, using the entry face for structure and counting and the action face for transformation.
aliases: the two faces of a matrix

nodes.name: Every matrix-work subspace is a null space
nodes.statement: In matrix work, every subspace encountered is a null space in disguise — the solution set of some A x = 0 — because such solution sets are exactly the homogeneous linear conditions on the coordinates.
aliases: every subspace you meet is a null space in disguise
